title: Being a Tourist
hint: Directions, tickets, prices and opening times; closed questions (Can I pay by card?), open questions (How do I get to ...?) and polite Could you tell me ...?
why: on holiday, almost everything starts with a question: where the station is, how much a ticket costs, what time the museum closes. If the question is clear and polite, people are happy to help, and you get the answer you need the first time.
know: Could you tell me ...? Do you know ...?
understand: Could you tell me where the station is?
able: ask for directions, prices, times and tickets, and understand the answers
check that you understood: So I turn left at the lights?
ask a stranger a question politely, without sounding too direct
mistakes: Could you tell me where is the station?
Could you tell me where the station is?
How much is it? / How much does it cost?
Do you know is there a bus?
Do you know if there is a bus?
warmup: Think of your last trip. What questions did you ask when you arrived?
Is it easy for you to ask a stranger for help in English? What do you say first?
What do you like to do in a new city: museums, food, walking, shopping?

say: Closed questions usually go up at the end (Can I pay by card? ↑); open questions usually go down (Where's the station? ↓). souvenir is soo-ve-NEER; queue sounds like the letter Q.

exercises.title: Questions and answers
exercises.intro: Match each question to its answer. Tap a question, then tap the answer.

items.l: How much is a return ticket?
items.why: How much asks about price, so the answer is an amount of money.

items.l: What time does the museum open?
items.why: What time asks for a time: At ten o'clock.

items.l: Which platform does the train leave from?
items.why: Which platform asks you to choose one platform: Platform 4.

items.l: How long does the tour take?
items.why: How long asks about time from start to end: About two hours.

items.l: Where can I buy a map?
items.why: Where asks about a place: At the tourist information desk.

items.l: Does this bus go to the airport?
items.why: A closed question with does. The short answer uses does too: Yes, it does.

items.l: Is it a single or a return?
items.why: An either/or question: the answer is one of the two choices.
A closed question with can: the answer is yes or no, then more information.
Open question in the present simple: What time + does + the museum + close?
Closed question with a normal verb (stop): Does + this train + stop?

exercises.title: Reading
exercises.text:
At the tourist office in Quebec City

Isla: Excuse me, do you speak English?

Assistant: Yes, of course. How can I help?

Isla: We're here for two days. What should we see first?

Assistant: Start with the old town. There's a guided walking tour at ten o'clock every morning. It takes about two hours.

Isla: How much is it?

Assistant: Twenty-five dollars for adults. You can buy tickets here.

Isla: Great. Can I pay by card?

Assistant: Yes, no problem.

Isla: And could you tell me how we get to the Citadel?

Assistant: Sure. Go straight on up this street, then turn left at the big hotel. The Citadel is on your right. It's about fifteen minutes on foot.

Isla: So we turn left at the hotel?

Assistant: Exactly. And don't miss the ferry to Lévis. It leaves every thirty minutes, and the view of the city from the river is beautiful.

Isla: Thank you so much!
exercises.intro: Read the conversation. Then type the missing word from the text, and press Check.

items.ask: What time does the walking tour start?
items.why: The assistant says: 'There's a guided walking tour at ten o'clock every morning.'

items.ask: How long does the tour take?
items.why: The assistant says: 'It takes about two hours.'

items.ask: How much is the tour for adults?
items.why: The assistant says: 'Twenty-five dollars for adults.'
The assistant says: 'turn left at the big hotel'. Isla checks: 'So we turn left at the hotel?'

items.ask: How often does the ferry leave?
items.why: The assistant says: 'It leaves every thirty minutes.'

exercises.title: Speaking
items: You are at a tourist office in a city you'd like to visit. Ask five questions to plan your day: two closed (Is there ...? Can I ...?) and three open (What ...? How much ...? How long ...?).
Role-play: you are lost. Stop a local politely, ask the way to the station, and check that you understood (So I go ...?).
Role-play: buy a train or bus ticket. Ask about the price, the time of the next one, the platform, and single or return.
Tell me about a time you asked for help on holiday. What did you ask? Was it easy to understand the answer?

parts.rule:
Watch out

  • closed: the answer is yes/no or one of two choices: Is this seat free? Single or return?
  • open: starts with a question word, and the answer is information: Where ...? How much ...?
  • polite indirect: starts with Could you tell me or Do you know, then normal word order
parts.intro: What kind of question is each one? Sort them.

chips.why: The answer is yes or no, so it is a closed question.
Does + subject + verb, and the answer is yes or no: a closed question.

chips.t: Is it a single or a return?
chips.why: An either/or question: the answer is one of two choices, so it is closed.
It starts with where, and the answer is a place: an open question.
How much asks for a price, so the answer is information: an open question.
What time asks for a time: an open question.
How long asks about time from start to end: an open question.

chips.t: Could you tell me where the bank is?
chips.why: Could you tell me + where + the bank is (normal order): a polite indirect question.

chips.t: Do you know if it's open?
chips.why: Do you know if + subject + verb: a polite indirect yes/no question.

chips.t: Do you know what time it closes?
chips.why: Do you know + what time + it closes (normal order): a polite indirect question.

items.why: A direct question needs the helper does: What time does the museum open?

items.q: Could you tell me where is the station?
items.why: After Could you tell me, use normal order: where the station is.
Say How much is it? (or How much does it cost?). Not 'How much costs it'.

items.q: Do you know if there's a bank near here?
items.why: Correct: Do you know if + there's + a bank. Normal order after Do you know.
In a direct question the helper comes first: Where can I buy tickets?

teacher.purpose: give learners the questions they need as tourists: directions, tickets, prices, times and opening hours. The grammar focus is question forms: closed questions (yes/no with the helper verb first, and either/or), open wh- questions (How do I get to ...? How much ...? How long ...? Which platform ...?) and polite indirect questions for strangers (Could you tell me where the station is? Do you know if ...?), plus checking that you understood.
teacher.before: choose a city the student would like to visit (or their own city) and have a map of it ready to share on screen. Print or prepare the role-play cards below.
plan: The three warm-up questions. Note every question the student makes and the word order they use; you will come back to these.

Travel words first, then the question table. Write one question of each kind on the board and ask: “Can you answer it with yes or no?” That is the closed/open test. Then the directions phrases with the map.
Matching, then the forms. In Exercise 2, ask the student to say each question aloud with the right intonation (up for closed, down for open).
Do one together and set the other for home.
The tourist office conversation. First ask: “Find two closed questions and two open questions in the text.” Then the five questions. Point out Isla's checking question: So we turn left at the hotel?
Role-plays with the cards below. You are the local or the ticket seller. Give directions with two or three steps so the student has to check (So I ...?).
Exercise 7 Part A together; Part B at home.
pron: Intonation: closed questions usually rise at the end (Can I pay by card? ↑), open questions usually fall (Where's the station? ↓). A rising open question can sound surprised or impatient.
Could you /ˈkʊdʒuː/: in fast speech it sounds like coojoo. Do you know often sounds like d'you know /djə ˈnəʊ/.
Excuse me /ɪkˈskjuːz mi/: stress on -cuse. The noun an excuse ends in /s/, the verb in /z/.
queue /kjuː/: like the letter Q; the extra letters are silent. admission /ədˈmɪʃən/: stress on -mi-.
What time does it: does it links to /dʌzɪt/. Students who say every word separately sound slower and more formal than they need to.
mistakes: Missing helper verb: What time the museum opens? Many languages make questions with intonation only. In English, a present simple question needs do / does: What time does the museum open? The -s moves to does.

Inversion after Could you tell me: Could you tell me where is the station? is the most common error at B1 and B2, even for strong students. The question is already in Could you tell me; the rest is normal order.
Do you know is there ...? For yes/no questions inside a polite opener, use if or whether: Do you know if there's a bus?
How much costs it? (Spanish ¿Cuánto cuesta?, French Combien ça coûte?). Teach How much is it? as a fixed phrase, and How much does it cost? for B2.
Subject questions (B2): Which bus goes to the airport? has no does, because which bus is the subject. Compare Which bus do I take? Mention only if the student is ready.
Too direct: Where is the toilet? is fine at a counter, but to a stranger in the street start with Excuse me or Sorry to bother you, and use Could you tell me ...?
Short answers: Does this bus go to the airport? Yes, it does. Not Yes, it goes. The short answer repeats the helper verb.
uk_us: Both are understood; Canadians usually say one-way.
A return in North America can sound like giving something back to a shop.
Downtown is the usual word in Canadian and US cities.
Canadians use both; schedule is more common for buses.
UK: join the queue; US/Canada: get in line, wait in line.
In Canada, washroom is the polite everyday word in public places.
adapt: Focus on ticket words (single, return, platform, timetable), opening hours, admission, and four direction phrases. Questions: is / does / can, and how do I get to, how much, what time.
All words; add a day pass, a connection, to change trains, to validate a ticket, accessible, wheelchair access. Add subject questions (Which bus goes ...?) and Would you happen to know ...?
Short role-plays with the cards; the student asks, you answer simply.
Longer role-plays with a problem: the tour is full, the train is cancelled, the price is different from the website. The student has to ask follow-up questions and check understanding.
teacher.extra:
Role-play cards

TouristLocal or staff
At the station. You want to go to Montreal and come back tomorrow. Ask about the price, the time of the next train and the platform. Pay by card if you can.Ticket office. Return to Montreal: $89 (one-way $52). Next train: 14:25, platform 3. Card is fine. The trip takes about five hours.
In the street. You are looking for the art gallery. Stop someone politely, ask the way, and check you understood.Local. Go straight on for two blocks, turn right at the bank, the gallery is on the left, opposite a park. About ten minutes on foot.
At the museum. Ask about opening hours, the price for adults, guided tours and where to buy souvenirs.Museum desk. Open 10:00 to 17:00, closed Mondays. Adults $20. Guided tour at 11:00 and 14:00, free with your ticket. Gift shop next to the exit.
prompts: Plan a day at the tourist office. Follow up with short answers so the student must ask more: “Yes, there is.” (“Where is it? How much is it?”). Count closed and open questions.
Asking the way. Give directions with three steps. Listen for a checking question (So I go ...?) and for Could you tell me where ... is? with normal order.
Buying a ticket. Follow up as the ticket seller: “Single or return?” “Today or tomorrow?” “Card or cash?” These either/or questions show how closed questions work.
A time you asked for help on holiday. Past questions: “What did you ask?” “Did they understand you?” “What would you say now?”

bank.why: Present simple question with a normal verb (take): How long does the ferry take?
After Do you know, use normal order: where the ticket office is.

bank.why: An either/or question joins two choices with or.

bank.q: How ___ is a coffee and a croissant?
bank.why: How much asks about price: How much is a coffee and a croissant?

bank.why: After Could you tell me, no does: Could you tell me what time the tour starts?

bank.q: ___ platform does the train to Montreal leave from?
bank.why: Which + noun asks you to choose one: Which platform?

bank.q: ___ does this bus go? To the airport or to the station?
bank.why: Where asks about a place: Where does this bus go?

bank.q: Do you know ___ there's a pharmacy near here?
bank.why: A polite yes/no question uses if (or whether): Do you know if there's a pharmacy?

bank.q: I'd like a ___ ticket to Halifax, please. I'm not coming back.
bank.why: A single (US/Canada one-way) ticket takes you there only.
How much asks about price: How much is the entrance fee?

bank.q: Sorry, could you say that ___? I didn't catch it.
bank.why: Could you say that again? asks someone to repeat.

bank.q: How long it takes to walk to the beach?
bank.why: A direct question needs does before the subject: How long does it take?

bank.q: Do you know is the castle open today?
bank.why: For a yes/no question after Do you know, use if + normal order: if the castle is open.

bank.q: Could you tell me how I get to the harbour?
bank.why: Correct: after Could you tell me, use normal order: how I get to the harbour.

bank.q: Where I can find a taxi?
bank.why: In a direct question the helper comes first: Where can I find a taxi?

bank.a: What time does the next boat leave?
bank.why: Open question: What time + does + subject + verb?

bank.a: Could you tell me how much this costs?
bank.why: Polite question: Could you tell me + how much + this costs (normal order, no does).

bank.a: Is there a cash machine near here?
bank.why: Closed question with there is: Is there + a thing + where?
